stem: Add \(5.55 \times 10^4\) and \(6.95 \times 10^3\), expressing the result in scientific notation.
solution:
For adding \(5.55 \times 10^4\) and \(6.95 \times 10^3\), first the exponent is made equal. Thus

\(5.55 \times 10^4 + 0.695 \times 10^4\). Then these numbers can be added as follows :

\((5.55 + 0.695) \times 10^4 = 6.245 \times 10^4\)
_note: p-01 right column, first pink box. The book prints NO `Solution :` label for Problems 2.1-2.4: the box is one continuous run of text that both poses and works the item. Split here at the natural seam — the imperative is the stem, the printed run is the solution verbatim. Nothing is dropped.

stem: Perform the subtraction \(3.5 \times 10^{-2} - 5.8 \times 10^{-3}\), expressing the result in scientific notation.
solution:
The subtraction of two numbers can be done as shown below:

\(3.5 \times 10^{-2} - 5.8 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(= (3.5 \times 10^{-2}) - (0.58 \times 10^{-2})\)

\(= (3.5 - 0.58) \times 10^{-2}\)

\(= 2.92 \times 10^{-2}\)
_note: p-01 right column, second pink box. No printed `Solution :` label — see the note on Solved Ex.2.1.

stem: In laboratory experiment, 10 g potassium chlorate sample on decomposition gives following data ; The sample contains 3.8 g of oxygen and the actual mass of oxygen in the quantity of potassium chlorate is 3.92 g. Calculate absolute error and relative error.
solution:
The observed is 3.8 g and accepted value is 3.92 g

Absolute error \(=\) Observed value \(-\) True value

\(= 3.8 - 3.92 = -0.12\ \mathrm{g}\)

The negative sign indicates that your experimental result is lower than the true value.

The relative error \(= \dfrac{\text{Absolute error}}{\text{True value}} \times 100\%\)

\(= \dfrac{-0.12}{3.92} \times 100\% = -3.06\%\)
_note: p-02 right column. The `10 g potassium chlorate` in the stem is not used anywhere in the printed working; transcribed as printed.

stem: The three identical samples of potassium chlorate are decomposed. The mass of oxygen is determined to be 3.87 g, 3.95 g and 3.89 g for the set. Calculate absolute deviation and relative deviation.
solution:
mean \(= \dfrac{3.87 + 3.95 + 3.89}{3} = 3.90\)

**Average deviation of a set of measurements**

| Sample | Mass of oxygen | Deviation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.87 g | 0.03 g |
| 2 | 3.95 g | 0.05 g |
| 3 | 3.89 g | 0.01 g |
| Mean absolute deviation | | 0.03 |

Absolute deviation \(= |\,\text{Observed value} - \text{Mean}\,|\)

\(\therefore\) Mean absolute deviation \(= \pm 0.03\ \mathrm{g}\).

The relative deviation,

\(= \dfrac{\text{Mean absolute deviation}}{\text{Mean}} \times 100\%\)

\(= \dfrac{0.03}{3.9} \times 100\% = 0.8\%\)
_note: p-03 left column. The book's table is reproduced as a GFM pipe table; its `Mean absolute deviation` row leaves the middle cell empty, as printed.

stem:
Round off each of the following to the number of significant digits indicated :

a. 1.223 to two digits

b. 12.56 to three digits

c. 122.17 to four digits

d. 231.5 to three digits.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: two defects in the book's printed answer to this worked example. (i) The question labels its four items a, b, c, d while the answer list labels them i, ii, iii, iv — the two are in the same order, so i corresponds to a and so on. (ii) The reasoning for item iii reads "the fifth digit is greater than 5, so we **do** it and add 1 to the fourth digit"; the intended word is **drop**, as it is in items i, ii and iv. All four rounded values — 1.2, 12.6, 122.2 and 232 — are correct.]

i. 1.2; the third digit is less than 5, so we drop it all the others to its right.

ii. 12.6 ; the fourth digit is greater than 5, so we drop it and add 1 to the third digit.

iii. 122.2 ; the fifth digit is greater than 5, so we do it and add 1 to the fourth digit.

iv. 232; the fourth digit is 5, so we drop it and add 1 to the third digit.
_note: p-04 left column. Transcribed verbatim, INCLUDING two printed defects: the stem labels its items a-d while the answer list labels them i-iv, and item iii reads 'we do it' where 'we drop it' is meant. Both carried to errata.

stem: A compound contains 4.07 % hydrogen, 24.27% carbon and 71.65 % chlorine by mass. Its molar mass is 98.96 g. What is its empirical formula ? Atomic masses of hydrogen, carbon and chlorine are 1.008, 12.000 and 35.453 u, respectively
solution:
[Textbook misprint: in Step III the book prints the divisor for carbon as 12.01 g, contradicting the atomic mass of 12.000 u its own stem supplies. The printed value 2.0225 is what 12.000 gives (24.27/12.000 = 2.0225); 12.01 would give 2.0208. So the divisor is the misprint and the value is right. The answer is unaffected either way — the H : C : Cl ratio is 2 : 1 : 1 and the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_4Cl_2}\) on both readings. The same 12.01 recurs in the empirical formula mass 49.48; with 12.000 it is 49.47, and the ratio 98.96/49.47 is still 2.]

**Step I :** Check whether the sum of all the percentages is 100.

\(4.07 + 24.27 + 71.65 = 99.99 \approx 100\)

Therefore no need to consider presence of oxygen atom in the molecule.

**Step II :** Conversion of mass percent to grams. Since we are having mass percent, it is convenient to use 100 g of the compound as the starting material. Thus in the 100 g sample of the above compound, 4.07 g hydrogen 24.27 g carbon and 71.65 g chlorine is present.

**Step III :** Convert into number/of moles of each element. Divide the masses obtained above by respective atomic masses of various elements.

Moles of hydrogen \(= \dfrac{4.07\ \mathrm{g}}{1.008\ \mathrm{g}} = 4.04\)

Moles of carbons \(= \dfrac{24.27\ \mathrm{g}}{12.01\ \mathrm{g}} = 2.0225\)

Moles of chlorine \(= \dfrac{71.65\ \mathrm{g}}{35.453\ \mathrm{g}} = 2.021\)

**Steps IV :** Divide the mole values obtained above by the smallest value among them. Since 2.021 is smallest value, division by it gives a ratio of 2:1:1 for H:C:Cl.

In case the ratio are not whole numbers, then they may be converted into whole number by multiplying by the suitable coefficient.

**Step V :** Write empirical formula by mentioning the numbers after writing the symbols of respective elements. \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\) is thus, the empirical formula of the above compound.

**Step VI :** Writing molecular formula

**a. Determine empirical formula mass :** Add the atomic masses of various atoms present in the empirical formula.

For \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\), empirical formula mass is

\(12.01 + 2 \times 1.008 + 35.453 = 49.48\ \mathrm{g}\)

**b. Divide molar mass by empirical formula mass**

\(\therefore\ \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{98.96\ \mathrm{g}}{49.48\ \mathrm{g}}\)

\(\therefore r = 2\)

**c. multiply empirical formula by r obtained above to get the molecular formula.**

Molecular formula \(= r \times\) empirical formula

molecular formula is \(2 \times \mathrm{CH_2Cl}\) i.e. \(\mathrm{C_2H_4Cl_2}\).
_note: Spans p-04 right column ('Contd on next page') into p-05 left column. Transcribed verbatim, INCLUDING the printed divisor 12.01 g in Step III, which contradicts the stem's stated atomic mass 12.000 u; the printed VALUE 2.0225 is what 12.000 gives (24.27/12.000 = 2.0225), while 12.01 gives 2.0208 — so the divisor is the misprint, not the value. Carried to errata; the answer is unaffected.

stem: A compound with molar mass 159 was found to contain 39.62 % copper and 20.13 % sulfur. Suggest molecular formula for the compound (Atomic masses: Cu = 63, S = 32 and O = 16).
solution:
% copper + % sulfur \(= 39.62 + 20.13 = 59.75\)

This is less than 100 % Hence compound contains adequate oxygen so that the total percentage of elements is 100%.

Hence % of oxygen \(= 100 - 59.75 = 40.25\%\)

Moles of Cu \(= \dfrac{\%\ \text{of Cu}}{\text{Atomic mass of Cu}} = \dfrac{39.62}{63} = 0.629\)

Moles of S \(= \dfrac{\%\ \text{of S}}{\text{Atomic mass of S}} = \dfrac{20.13}{32} = 0.629\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{\%\ \text{of O}}{\text{Atomic mass of O}} = \dfrac{40.25}{16} = 2.516\)

Hence the ratio of number of moles of Cu:S:O is

\(\dfrac{0.629}{0.629} = 1\), \(\dfrac{0.629}{0.629} = 1\) and \(\dfrac{2.516}{0.629} = 4\)

Hence empirical formula is \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\)

Empirical formula mass \(= 63 + 32 + 16 \times 4 = 159\)

Molar mass = Empirical mass (Since Molar mass = Molecular mass)

\(\therefore\) Molecular formula = Empirical formula \(= \mathrm{CuSO_4}\)
_note: p-05 right column.

stem: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide and water formed on complete combustion of 24 g of methane gas. (Atomic masses, C = 12 u, H = 1 u, O = 16 u)
solution:
The balanced chemical equation is,

\(\mathrm{CH_4(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\)

\((12+4)\quad 2 \times (16 \times 2)\quad 12 + (16 \times 2)\quad 2 \times (2+16)\)

\(= 16\ \mathrm{g}\quad = 64\ \mathrm{g}\quad = 44\ \mathrm{g}\quad = 36\ \mathrm{g}\)

Hence, 16 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) on complete combustion will produce 44 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

\(\therefore\) 24 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4} = \dfrac{24}{16} \times 44 = 66\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

Similarly, 16 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) will produce 36 g of water.

24 g of \(\mathrm{CH_4} \equiv \dfrac{24}{16} \times 36 = 54\ \mathrm{g}\) water.
_note: p-06 left column, bottom box.

stem: How much CaO will be produced by decomposition of 5g \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) ?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed final line reads "= 2.8 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\)", which contradicts its own question — the stem asks how much CaO is produced, and the line's own arithmetic (56/100 × 5 g) is the CaO fraction. As printed it asserts that decomposing 5 g of calcium carbonate yields 2.8 g of calcium carbonate. The species has been corrected to CaO above; the value 2.8 g is the book's and is correct.]

Calcium carbonate decomposes according to the balanced equation,

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ } \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

\(40 + 12 + 3 \times 16 \qquad 40 + 16 \qquad 12 + 2 \times 16\)

\(= 100\) parts \(\qquad = 56\) parts \(\qquad = 44\) parts

So, 100 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) produces 56 g of CaO

\(\therefore\) 5 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) will produce

\(= \dfrac{56\ \mathrm{g}}{100\ \mathrm{g}} \times 5\,\mathrm{g} = 2.8\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{CaO}\)
_note: p-06 right column, top box. Transcribed VERBATIM including the defect in the last line: the book writes '2.8 g of CaCO3' where the quantity computed — and the quantity the stem asks for — is CaO. The VALUE 2.8 g is correct. Repaired via solved-fixes + errata, per the brief.

stem: How many litres of oxygen at STP are required to burn completely 2.2 g of propane, \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\) ?
solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of propane is,

\(\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

\(3 \times 12 + 8 \times 1 \qquad 5 \times 22.4\ \mathrm{L}\)

\((44\ \mathrm{g}) \qquad (112\ \mathrm{L})\)

(Where 1 mol of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L of volume)

Thus 44 g of propane requires 112 litres of oxygen for complete combustion

\(\therefore\) 2.2 g of propane will require

\(\dfrac{112}{44} \times 2.2 = 5.6\) litres of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at STP for complete combustion.
_note: p-06 right column, middle box.

stem: A piece of zinc weighing 0.635 g when treated with excess of dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) liberated \(200\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of hydrogen at STP. Calculate the percentage purity of the zinc sample.
solution:
The relevant balanced chemical equation is,

\(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2}\)

It indicates that 22.4 L of hydrogen at STP \(= 65\ \mathrm{g}\) of Zn.

(where Atomic mass of Zn = 65 u)

\(\therefore\) 0.200 L of hydrogen at STP

\(= \dfrac{65\ \mathrm{g}}{22.4\ \mathrm{L}} \times 0.200\ \mathrm{L} = 0.58\ \mathrm{g}\)

\(\therefore\) percentage purity of Zn \(= \dfrac{0.58}{0.635} \times 100 = 91.33\%\)
_note: p-06 right column, bottom box.

stem:
Urea \([(\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}]\) is prepared by reacting ammonia with carbon dioxide.

\(2\,\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

In one process, 637.2 g of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) are treated with 1142 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). (a) Which of the two reactants is the limiting reagent ? (b) Calculate the mass of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) formed. (c) How much excess reagent (in grams) is left at the end of the reaction ?
solution:
[Textbook note (not an error): the book sets the part labels (a) and (b) inline in the middle of a sentence, so the line prints as "...because it produces (a) smaller amount of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)) (b) The molar mass..." — the (a) stands where the article "a" belongs, there is an unmatched closing bracket, and part (b) starts mid-sentence. The layout has been restored above so the three parts read as parts; every number, quantity and conclusion is the book's own and is unchanged.]

(a) We carry out two separate calculations. First : If 637.2 g of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) reacts completely, calculate the number of moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\), that could be produced, by the following relation.

mass of \(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow\) moles of \(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow\) moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} = 637.2\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{NH_3} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{NH_3}}{17.03\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{NH_3}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}}{2\ \text{mol } \mathrm{NH_3}}\)

\(= 18.71\) moles \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

Second : The relation from 1142 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\):

mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow\) moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow\) moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

The number of moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) that could be produced if all the \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) reacted :

moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} = 1142\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{CO_2} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}{44.01\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}}{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}\)

\(= 25.95\) mol \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

It follows, therefore, that \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) must be the limiting reagent because it produces a smaller amount of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\).

(b) The molar mass of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) is 60.06 g. We use this as a conversion factor to convert from moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\) to grams of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\).

mass of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} = 18.71\ \text{mol}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} \times \dfrac{60.06\ \mathrm{g}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}}{1\ \text{mol}}\)

\(\therefore = 1124\ \mathrm{g}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)

(c) Starting with 18.71 moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\), we can determine the mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) that reacted using the mole ratio from the balanced equation and the molar mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

The conversion steps are

moles of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} \longrightarrow\) moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow\) grams of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

So that,

mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) reacted \(= 18.71\ \text{mol}\ (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}{1\ \text{mol } (\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}} \times \dfrac{44.01\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}}{1\ \text{mol } \mathrm{CO_2}}\)

\(= 823.4\ \mathrm{g}\)

The amount of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) remaining (in excess) is the difference between the initial amount (1142 g) and the amount reacted (823.4 g):

mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) remaining \(= 1142\ \mathrm{g} - 823.4\ \mathrm{g} = 318.6\ \mathrm{g} \approx 319\ \mathrm{g}\)
_note: Spans p-07 (left column bottom box + whole right column, 'Contd. on next page') into p-08 left column top box. Transcribed VERBATIM, including the printed line '...because it produces (a) smaller amount of (NH2)2CO) (b) The molar mass...', where the part labels (a)/(b) are set inline mid-sentence and there is an unmatched closing bracket. Re-laid out via solved-fixes + errata so the repair is auditable rather than silent.

stem: A solution is prepared by adding 2 g of a substance A to 18 g of water. Calculate the mass percent of the solute.
solution:
Mass percent of A \(= \dfrac{\text{Mass of A}}{\text{Mass of solution}} \times 100\)

\(= \dfrac{2\ \mathrm{g}}{2\ \mathrm{g}\ \text{of A} + 18\ \mathrm{g}\ \text{of water}} \times 100\)

\(= \dfrac{2\ \mathrm{g}}{20\ \mathrm{g}} \times 100 = 10\%\)
_note: p-08 left column, bottom box.

stem: Calculate the molarity of NaOH in the solution prepared by dissolving its 4 g in enough water to form 250 mL of the solution.
solution:
Since molarity (M) \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = \dfrac{\text{Mass of NaOH / Molar mass of NaOH}}{0.250\ \mathrm{L}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = \dfrac{4\ \mathrm{g}\,/\,40\ \mathrm{g}}{0.250\ \mathrm{L}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = \dfrac{0.1\ \mathrm{mol}}{0.250\ \mathrm{L}}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{M} = 0.4\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}} = 0.4\ \mathrm{M}\)

Note that molarity of a solution depends upon temperature because volume of a solution is temperature dependent.
_note: p-08 right column.

stem: The density of 3M solution of NaCl is \(1.25\ \mathrm{g\ mL^{-1}}\) Calculate molality of the solution.
solution:
Molarity \(= 3\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

Mass of NaCl in 1 L solution \(= 3 \times 58.5\)

\(\therefore = 175.5\ \mathrm{g}\)

Mass of 1L solution \(= 1000 \times 1.25 = 1250\ \mathrm{g}\)

\((\because\) density \(= 1.25\ \mathrm{g\ mL^{-1}})\)

Mass of water in solution \(= 1250 - 175.5\)

\(\therefore = 1074.5\ \mathrm{g}\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\)

\(= \dfrac{3\ \mathrm{mol}}{1.0745\ \mathrm{kg}} = 2.79\ \mathrm{m}\)
_note: p-09 left column.
